title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Nov 10, 2026
intro: Handoffs are this week's weak point: summaries lose task detail, invent permissions, and replay approved actions.

cards.title: Pass the full task file to every agent in a multi-agent pipeline
cards.problem: A planner–coder–reviewer team passed 25.7% of hidden acceptance tests versus 56.8% for one agent, because only the planner saw the task.
cards.apply: Give the coder and reviewer the original task file alongside the planner summary. Benchmark the team against a single agent at equal spend before keeping the extra roles.
cards.result: In the source experiment, sharing the task file lifted the team to 54.1%, level with one agent, though still at higher cost.

evidence.note: The author measured pass rates on six feature tasks with Codex.

cards.title: Compact agent history to a short context instead of paying for long windows
cards.problem: Long-context serving is priced up to 7x more per token, yet agents rarely use the extra window.
cards.apply: Summarize the agent history on a fixed cadence and cap working context near 16K tokens. Run your own eval against the full-context baseline before switching.
cards.result: NVIDIA reports little accuracy loss on Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol at 16K with frequent compaction, at a fraction of the serving cost.

evidence.note: NVIDIA preprint "You don't need long context" reports the accuracy and cost result.

cards.title: Audit compaction summaries for permissions the history never granted
cards.problem: A self-written handoff summary can state permissions or requirements the original record does not support, and the next step then obeys them.
cards.apply: Treat summaries as untrusted input: diff any permission, approval, or policy sentence against the source history, and drop unsupported ones before resuming.
cards.result: Compacted runs stop inheriting invented authorizations, so tool-call gates keep matching what the user actually approved.

evidence.note: The paper studies unsupported policy statements in handoff summaries; the mitigation is an editorial inference.

cards.title: Make approved tool calls run at most once across crashes
cards.problem: After a crash and documented resume, one approved payment ran twice in LangGraph, Pydantic AI and the OpenAI Agents SDK.
cards.apply: Key each approved side-effecting call by an idempotency ID and record it before executing. On resume, skip any ID already recorded.
cards.result: The source claims approved tool calls run at most once, which makes retries after a crash safe.

evidence.note: The Call4Agents write-up reproduces duplicate payments in three frameworks.

cards.title: Carry source ACLs onto every memory note your agent synthesizes
cards.problem: Metadata filters block 100% of unauthorized raw-chunk queries, yet cross-document synthesis leaked confidential parent secrets in 2 of 3 background tasks.
cards.apply: Stamp each synthesized memory note with the intersection of its parents' permissions, and filter memory recall by the requesting user the same way as raw retrieval.
cards.result: Unprivileged users stop retrieving executive data through derived notes. Re-run the benchmark linter to confirm a 0% leak rate.

evidence.note: The benchmark reports 0% raw-RAG leaks versus 67% agent-memory leaks.

cards.title: Let the agent express a bulk workflow as one program, not per-node tool calls
cards.problem: Bulk edits like replacing a brand color across thousands of nodes force a model round trip per decision.
cards.apply: Expose the document API to a sandboxed script. Have the agent write one program that inspects, decides and applies the changes, and start execution while it streams.
cards.result: Framer reports the rebuilt harness is up to 33% cheaper and 20% faster.

evidence.note: Framer states the cost and latency figures for its own agent harness.
